text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's Austrian newspapers:

- Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky told the paper in an interview the defence Ministry will not receive any extra funds for the planned controversial purchase of defence aircraft, but must remain within the existing budget.
- Vienna Bourse head Gerard Randa says new life must be breathed into the stock exchange in 1997 in spite of competition from European markets.
- Sales in champagne and sparkling wine rose in Austria this year but Austrian producers are battling against high tax conditions and bootleg imports.

- The paper says the cards in the long-running Creditanstalt privatisation saga have merely been reshuffled after Finance Minister Viktor Klima reopened the tender on Friday to allow current bidders to improve their offers.

- A proposal apparently favoured by economic minister Johannes Farnleitner to float Austria's second biggest bank Creditanstalt on the stock exchange would cut proceeds from the sale by two billion schillings, Finance Minister Klima claims.
- The Vienna bourse is worth one billion schillings. Klima heralds a new era for the bourse with a restructuring and an increase in budget.
- WIFO economist Jan Stankovsky estimates the expansion of the European Union to include former communist countries will cost 229 billion schillings and should be done in stages.

- EU commissioner Franz Fischler strongly criticised his own conservative People's Party for siding with the far right Freedom Party over the issue of the sale of Creditanstalt, saying it was not constructive in the current coalition.
- An "Index of Authoritarianism" study shows Austrians want more authority and strong man leadership.
- Bidders for Creditanstalt will only be able to raise their prices as a way of improving their offers. But there is speculation there could be a change of partners among the candidates.
- Editorial says Chancellor Vranitzky wants a "new strong European Bank" in which even small-time savers can have shares.
